title: The generalized tangent bound
subtitle: G2 lecture 127000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: The single-angle tangent theorem controls a tangent of the subspace error when spectral separation is measured from a Rayleigh–Ritz compression.
body: Davis and Kahan's Theorem six point three develops this geometry in a generalized form. The trial space may have smaller dimension than the exact selected space, and the conclusion concerns a directed tangent. A tangent bound is stronger than a sine bound when the angle is large. Yet the theorem does not simply divide a previously known sine estimate by a cosine. The Rayleigh–Ritz orthogonality and the placement of the unwanted spectrum do additional work.

slides.title: Which spaces are being compared?
body: Let V be an exact reducing subspace, with complementary space W. Let Z be a trial subspace with an orthonormal coordinate map. We do not initially require Z and V to have equal dimension. Compress A to Z. The result is the Rayleigh–Ritz operator A zero. Assume its spectrum lies at or below an upper threshold alpha. Assume the spectrum of A on the unwanted exact complement W lies at or above alpha plus delta, where delta is positive. This is the source's one-sided separation. The trial compression is below; the unwanted exact spectrum is above. The subspace V itself may have a larger dimension than Z, and its exact spectrum need not consist of one eigenvalue.

slides.title: Why a right angle is impossible
slides.lead: Suppose a nonzero trial vector z lies entirely in W.
body: Because the Rayleigh–Ritz compression has spectrum at most alpha, its quadratic form on z is at most alpha times the squared length of z. But because z also belongs to W and A restricted to W is bounded below by alpha plus delta, the same quadratic form is at least alpha plus delta times its squared length. This is impossible for positive delta. Hence Z has no nonzero vector perpendicular to V. In finite dimension, the projection from Z into V is therefore injective and bounded below. We can regard Z as a graph over its image in V. Its graph map gives a finite tangent angle operator.

slides.title: A principal-vector calculation
slides.lead: Choose a unit trial vector z realizing the largest directed principal angle theta in the finite-dimensional case.
body: Write it as cosine theta times a unit vector v in V, plus sine theta times a unit vector w in W. The chosen directions are principal vectors, so projection of w back onto Z is sine theta times z. Let T be the Rayleigh–Ritz compression of A to Z. Since z is in Z, the quadratic form of T at z is at most alpha. Since w is in W, the quadratic form of A at w is at least alpha plus delta. Take the inner product of the residual R z with w. The A term contributes sine theta times the quadratic form of A at w.

slides.title: Check the bound on a rotated line
slides.lead: Take A diagonal with eigenvalues zero and d, with d positive.
body: The exact selected subspace is the horizontal axis, and W is the vertical axis. Let the one-dimensional trial subspace be the line at angle theta above the horizontal. Its Ritz value is d times sine squared theta. The unwanted exact eigenvalue is d, so the gap between that eigenvalue and the Ritz compression is d cosine squared theta. The Ritz residual has length d sine theta cosine theta. Multiply the spectral gap by tangent theta. We get d cosine squared theta times sine theta divided by cosine theta, which equals d sine theta cosine theta. Equality holds.

slides.title: Why the full theorem needs singular-value machinery
slides.lead: Our principal-vector proof controlled the largest tangent, hence the operator norm.
body: A theorem for every unitarily invariant norm requires considerably more: the sum of the first k tangent singular values must be bounded by the corresponding residual singular-value prefix, for each k. It is not sufficient to apply the operator-norm proof independently to each singular direction. The Ritz compression can mix those directions, and the extremizing subspaces can differ with k. The full proof uses finite-rank variational principles, compression identities, and Ky Fan dominance to control all prefixes simultaneously.

slides.title: Dimensions and the precise tangent theorem
slides.lead: The printed generalized theorem uses a strict dimension inequality between the trial and exact selected coordinate spaces.
body: In the common finite-dimensional situation, a smaller trial space can still be compared with the larger selected exact space through directed principal angles. The equal-rank tangent theorem is a separate companion, not a consequence of specializing a strict inequality. Extensions to arbitrary trial dimension require explicit transversality and ideal hypotheses and must be stated separately. The finite-dimensional strict-lower-rank, equal-rank, and Hilbert-space statements have different assumptions.

slides.title: Domain and norm requirements
slides.lead: For an unbounded self-adjoint A, the trial subspace must lie in its domain, and the Ritz compression and residual must be bounded in the appropriate senses.
body: The exact spectral complement needs to reduce A. The gap must compare the actual Ritz compression spectrum with the unwanted exact spectrum. For a chosen symmetric ideal, finiteness of the residual ideal norm is a hypothesis and finiteness of the tangent ideal norm is part of the conclusion. The Lyapunov or Sylvester steps that lead to the all-prefix bound must respect the same norm class. The generalized tangent theorem therefore involves more than an angle identity.

slides.title: Close
body: Compare a principal direction's unwanted spectral energy with its Ritz energy. Use residual orthogonality to gain a cosine factor. Divide to obtain tangent rather than sine. Then extend from the largest principal angle to all singular-value prefixes using the Ky Fan machinery.
